Invoicer · Procedure

Raising an invoice, and getting paid

Twenty steps from an empty page to money recorded against the invoice. Every step is one action, with the screen you should be looking at when you have done it. Follow it start to finish the first time; after that you will only need the pictures.

Walked
6 September 2026
Worked example
SATC-2026-0184
Invoice total
$3,068.89
Time, once known
about four minutes

The route, before the detail

  1. /generator The editor type the invoice
  2. PDF A file check the layout
  3. /signup An account to keep and send it
  4. /invoice/1 Your invoice saved, with a number
  5. email The client email, link and PDF
  6. Paid The money recorded against it
Steps 01–07

Build the invoice — no account needed

01

Open the editor

Go to /generator. You do not sign in, and you are not asked to.

A correct screen

An invoice fills the page, already dated today and numbered INV-0001. The page you are looking at is the document — there is no separate form. The panel on the right offers 48 designs, a logo upload, and a note saying nothing is saved until you ask.

02

Type your own details, at the top left

Click Your business name and type. Press Tab or click the grey lines under it for the address; each line is its own line on the printed page.

A correct screen

Your name goes bold at the top and the address sits under it in grey. Nothing jumps or reflows anywhere else.

03

Type who it goes to

Fill BILL TO the same way — name, then address, then their email. Then set the invoice number, and the terms if they are not Net 14.

A correct screen

The client's name is bold under BILL TO, and the invoice number you typed replaces INV-0001 in the top right. Leave SHIP TO alone unless it differs — it prints nothing when empty.

04

Add the work, one line at a time

Type into the first row, then press + Add a line for each further item. Quantity takes decimals — 1.5 for an hour and a half.

A correct screen

Each row's AMOUNT is quantity × unit price and updates as you type; the Subtotal underneath follows immediately. In the example: 1,450 + 1,155 + 330 = $2,935.00.

05

Add tax, and a discount if you are giving one

Type the tax rate into the Tax box. The % next to each of Discount and Tax is a dropdown — switch it to $ for a flat amount.

A correct screen

Discount comes off the subtotal before tax is worked out. Here: 2,935 − 100 = 2,835, then 8.25% of that is 233.89, so the Total is $3,068.89. Check the Total, not just the boxes — that is the number the client pays.

Watch out

The Notes and Terms blocks on the left show grey example wording. That is a prompt, not content: leave them and they print nothing at all. Type into them if you want the client to see them.

06

Choose a design

Pick a family across the top of the panel — Classic, Band, Minimal, Bold, Stripe, Modern — then a colour. The grid scrolls; there are eight colours in each of the six families.

A correct screen

The document restyles instantly and every word you have typed stays put. Switching designs never costs you work, so try several.

07

Download the PDF

Press Download PDF, top right. No account, no email address.

A correct screen

The file downloads named after your invoice number. Your draft stays on the page and in this browser — reloading will not lose it.

Watch out

The PDF from this page carries a DRAFT badge and there is no way to turn it off here. Do not send this file to a client. Use it to check the layout, then follow the rest of this procedure to send the real one.

Steps 08–14

Keep it, and send it

08

Create an account

Press Save & send it. Fill in your business name, work email and a password of at least eight characters, tick the agreement, and press Create account.

A correct screen

Nothing you typed on the invoice is asked for again — the account is separate from the document.

09

You land on Account, not back on your invoice

Read the two yellow notices, then leave this page. There is nothing to fill in here yet.

A correct screen

A green Welcome! Your account is ready. The two yellow notices are about the site as a whole, not your account: Stripe is not connected, so clients cannot pay online, and email is not set up until the administrator configures it.

Watch out

Signing up does not bring you back to the invoice you were building, and there is no link to the editor anywhere once you are signed in. Type /generator in the address bar to get back to it — that is step 10.

10

Go back to the editor — your draft is still there

Put /generator in the address bar.

A correct screen

Everything is exactly as you left it: both addresses, all three lines, the tax, the discount and the design. The draft is held in this browser, so it survives the trip through sign-up — but only in this browser on this machine.

11

Save it to your invoices

The top-right button now reads Save to my invoices. Press it.

A correct screen

The button changed because you are signed in. This is the first moment anything is written down.

12

Check the invoice page

Read the figures against what you meant to bill, before anyone else sees them.

A correct screen

Invoice saved. The invoice has a number, a status of Draft, a balance due, and an Activity list on the right that will record everything that happens to it from here.

Watch out

This page shows the invoice in the default navy, not the design you chose. The design is applied to the PDF only.

13

Send it

The client's email is already in the box. Change it if it should go to someone else, then press Send invoice.

A correct screen

One button, one recipient. The PDF is attached for you — you do not download and attach it yourself.

14

Confirm it went

Read the Activity list on the right.

A correct screen

The status moves from Draft to Sent, Activity gains Invoice sent — to and the address, and the button becomes Resend invoice. If sending fails you get a red message saying why; nothing is silent.

Steps 15–20

What the client gets, and getting paid

15

What lands in their inbox

Nothing to do. This is what you have just sent, so you know what they are looking at.

A correct screen

Your business name in the subject and the greeting, the amount and due date side by side, and a button. The invoice number and terms are on the line under it, and the PDF is attached. The footer carries your address, not ours.

16

The page behind the button

You can see it yourself any time from Preview client view on the invoice page.

A correct screen

The amount due and the date, then the whole invoice. The client needs no account and no password. When online payment is switched on, a Pay button sits beside the amount at the top; with Stripe not connected, it correctly does not appear.

17

The PDF attached to the email

Open the attachment on the email you sent, and look at it before you rely on it.

A correct screen

The design you chose, the same figures, and your details in the footer.

Watch out

The attached copy is stamped DRAFT, because the file is made a moment before the invoice's status changes to Sent. Download the PDF again from the invoice page and it reads SENT. Until this is fixed, send the second one by hand if the client's accounts department is strict.

18

When the money arrives, record it

On the invoice page press Mark as paid. Use this for a bank transfer, a cheque, or cash — anything that did not come through the site.

A correct screen

One button. You do not type the amount; it settles the whole balance.

19

Check it settled

Read the panel and the Activity list.

A correct screen

Invoice marked as paid. The status is Paid, the panel turns green and reads Paid in full with the date, Balance due is $0.00, and Activity gains Marked paid. A Mark as unpaid button appears in case you pressed it too early.

20

Check the workspace totals

Click Invoices in the top bar.

A correct screen

Four figures across the top — outstanding, overdue, paid, and how many invoices you have. After the payment above, outstanding reads $0.00 and paid reads the invoice total. The list underneath filters by status, and Export CSV takes the lot.

Using this again

This is also the regression check. Walk it after a change and every step either matches its picture or does not — and a step that no longer matches is either a fault in the product or an out-of-date instruction here. Finding out which is the job.

The three Watch out notes are not mistakes you have made. They are known faults, written up separately for whoever fixes them, and repeated here so nobody spends ten minutes looking for a setting that does not exist.
